content: Premenstrual syndrome (PMS), also referred to as premenstrual tension (PMT), is a condition characterized by a range of physical, psychological, and emotional symptoms that are closely associated with a woman’s menstrual cycle. While the majority of women of reproductive age experience some premenstrual symptoms, PMS is specifically diagnosed when these symptoms are severe enough to interfere with daily life. These symptoms are predictable, occurring consistently during the luteal phase, which is the two weeks leading up to menstruation. Symptoms may resolve once menstruation begins, but in some cases, they can persist even after bleeding has started. Irritability is a common feature during PMS. Approximately 14% of women aged 20 to 35 experience symptoms so severe that they are unable to attend work or school. In extreme cases, PMS symptoms can be disabling, and this severe form is classified as premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD), which has its own psychiatric designation. In the United States, the term PMS is widely recognized and often used colloquially to describe menstrual-related difficulties, though its usage in casual settings may not align with the clinical definition. The precise cause of PMS remains unclear. Although PMS is associated with the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle, hormone levels in affected women are typically within normal ranges. The condition appears to have a genetic component, as it is more common among twins. Current research suggests that interactions between sex hormones and neurotransmitters in the central nervous system, particularly serotonin, may play a role. Certain hormonal medications, such as ethynodiol diacetate and ethinyl estradiol, have been implicated in causing PMS. There is no definitive laboratory test or physical finding to confirm a diagnosis of PMS. Physicians often ask patients to maintain a prospective record of their symptoms over at least two menstrual cycles to establish a pattern of predictably recurring symptoms. This helps differentiate PMS from other conditions that may mimic its symptoms. Several standardized tools, such as the Calendar of Premenstrual Syndrome Experiences (COPE), the Prospective Record of the Impact and Severity of Menstruation (PRISM), and the Visual Analogue Scales (VAS), are available to document and assess PMS symptoms. It is important to rule out other medical conditions that may worsen during menstruation, a phenomenon known as menstrual magnification. Disorders such as depression, migraines, seizure disorders, chronic fatigue syndrome, irritable bowel syndrome, asthma, and allergies can be exacerbated during the menstrual cycle and may be mistaken for PMS. A distinguishing feature of these conditions is that they are not confined to the luteal phase. Stress is also a known factor that increases the likelihood of PMS. PMS encompasses a wide range of symptoms, with over 150 distinct symptoms identified. The severity and specific symptoms vary between individuals and even from one cycle to the next. Common symptoms include abdominal bloating, breast tenderness, stress, anxiety, depression, crying spells, mood swings, irritability, anger, changes in appetite, food cravings, insomnia, joint or muscle pain, headaches, fatigue, acne, breast swelling, difficulty concentrating, social withdrawal, increased body temperature, and exacerbation of pre-existing skin, respiratory, or eye conditions. Treatment for PMS involves a combination of lifestyle modifications, supportive therapies, and medical interventions. Supportive therapy, including counseling, reassurance, and education, is essential to help patients regain control over their lives. Aerobic exercise has been shown to alleviate some symptoms. Lifestyle changes, such as reducing caffeine, sugar, and sodium intake, increasing dietary fiber, and ensuring adequate rest, may also provide relief. Calcium supplementation (1200 mg/day) and vitamin E (400 IU/day) have demonstrated some efficacy in clinical studies. Other supplements, such as vitamin B6, magnesium, manganese, and tryptophan, have been suggested, though evidence supporting their effectiveness is limited. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are considered the first-line pharmacological treatment for severe PMS. Fluoxetine, at doses of 20-60 mg/day, is the most extensively studied SSRI, but other options include sertraline, paroxetine, clomipramine, fluvoxamine, and nefazodone. These medications can be administered continuously or intermittently, depending on symptom recurrence. Hormonal interventions, such as combined oral contraceptives or contraceptive patches, are commonly used. Progesterone therapy has been employed for years, but its efficacy remains inconclusive. In severe cases, gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) agonists may be prescribed, though they carry significant side effects. Diuretics, such as spironolactone, have been used to manage water retention, and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), such as ibuprofen, can address pain. Evening primrose oil, which contains gamma-linolenic acid (GLA), has been advocated by some, but scientific evidence supporting its use is lacking. There is ongoing debate regarding the nature of PMS. Some medical professionals argue that PMS may be a socially constructed disorder, while others emphasize its medical validity, particularly in light of the well-established diagnosis of PMDD. PMDD is associated with measurable changes in serotonin precursors, as demonstrated by positron emission tomography (PET) studies, and responds consistently to SSRI treatment. Critics of the PMS diagnosis suggest that it may be overdiagnosed or misdiagnosed, with other conditions such as chronic depression or frustration being incorrectly attributed to PMS. Additionally, cultural factors may influence the perception and reporting of PMS symptoms, particularly in Western societies where awareness of the condition is widespread. The lack of rigorous scientific studies on the emotional aspects of PMS further complicates the debate.
